summary: Discusses how operators of wireline networks can introduce IPv6 incrementally while continuing to support IPv4, even as IPv4 addresses run out. It describes the challenges and approaches. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: Changing to a new kind of road must be done bit by bit while cars keep driving. This memo explains how network companies can do that.

subtitle: Phased approaches for IPv6 deployment in broadband networks.

tldr.problem: Broadband operators must deploy IPv6 to keep services operational as IPv4 addresses run out, but legacy devices and applications require continued IPv4 support during an extended transition.
tldr.mechanism: This memo outlines a phased approach progressing through foundation work, tunneled IPv6, native dual stack, and finally IPv6-only operation, using commercially available transition technologies appropriate to each phase.
tldr.outcome: Operators can move from IPv4-only networks toward IPv6-dominant environments incrementally, managing costs and operational complexity while maintaining service quality.

facts.label: Typical timeline
facts.value: 7-10 years to IPv6-only, varies by operator

facts.label: Key technologies
facts.value: 6rd, Native Dual Stack, CGN/NAT444, DS-Lite, NAT64

today: RFC 6782 remains valid guidance for broadband operators planning IPv6 transitions. Published in November 2012, it has not been obsoleted and continues to reflect the phased approach most operators have adopted.

sections.title: The IPv6 Transition Challenge
sections.content:
Wireline broadband operators face a difficult situation. IPv4 addresses are running out, making it impossible to assign new devices without reusing addresses (carrier-grade NAT). IPv6 is necessary for long-term connectivity, but deployment is complex and risky. Legacy devices (older computers, printers, gaming consoles) support only IPv4. Content remains partially IPv4-only. Operators must meet all these requirements simultaneously.

This document addresses operators of cable, DSL, and fiber access networks. It assumes the operator controls the core network, can deploy dual stack infrastructure, and wants to minimize service disruption while transitioning from IPv4-only to IPv6-dominant.
sections.plainLanguage: Broadband companies must switch to a new internet standard, but millions of old devices still need the old standard. They can't force everyone to buy new gear at once.

sections.title: A Phased Transition Model
sections.content:
Rather than attempting a single cut-over, operators should follow a series of phases matched to network maturity and market readiness. Phase 0 (Foundation) establishes the prerequisites: staff training, system assessment, routing infrastructure, security policies, transition architecture planning, and management tools. These foundational steps are essential but not visible to subscribers.

Phase 1 (Tunneled IPv6) provides early IPv6 connectivity while the access network remains IPv4-only. 6to4 relays offer automatic tunneling, while 6rd (IPv6 Rapid Deployment) provides more controlled tunneled access. Phase 2 (Native Dual Stack) delivers native IPv6 to subscriber CPEs alongside native IPv4. Phase 3 (IPv6-Only) removes IPv4 from subscriber access, using DS-Lite for IPv4 content reach or NAT64 for IPv6-to-IPv4 translation.
sections.plainLanguage: The plan has clear stages: get ready, offer IPv6 through tunnels, offer both IPv4 and IPv6 natively, then eventually drop IPv4 from subscriber gear but keep reaching IPv4 servers.

sections.title: Early Transition: Phase 1 and Phase 2
sections.content:
Phase 1 uses tunneling to deliver IPv6 through existing IPv4 infrastructure. Automatic mechanisms (6to4, Teredo) work without configuration but may have performance issues. 6rd is more controlled and scales better: the operator deploys relays, CPEs send IPv6 packets encapsulated over IPv4 to the relay, which decapsulates and forwards to the IPv6 network. The IPv6 prefix is derived from the subscriber's IPv4 address, making operational tools straightforward.

Phase 2 (Native Dual Stack) is the preferred long-term direction. Operators deploy IPv6 through the entire network (core, peering, and access) and provide IPv6 addresses and prefixes to subscribers via DHCPv6. Both IPv4 and IPv6 traffic flow natively without translation. This requires upgrading core routers, peering infrastructure, DNS, DHCP, and management systems. Early IPv6 traffic volumes will be low while operators optimize IPv6 content and services, but dual stack is stable and sustainable.
sections.plainLanguage: At first, IPv6 is wrapped inside IPv4 packets and sent through existing plumbing. Then, the network installs new pipes that carry both IPv4 and IPv6 side by side, which is cleaner and faster.

sections.title: Supporting IPv4 After Exhaustion
sections.content:
Once IPv4 addresses run out, operators cannot assign unique public addresses to new devices. Carrier-Grade NAT (CGN/NAT444) allows address sharing: multiple subscriber CPEs receive private addresses, and a carrier NAT translates them to a smaller pool of public addresses. CGN can be deployed alongside native dual stack (dual stack with CGN on the IPv4 path, native IPv6 on the IPv6 path).

DS-Lite (Dual-Stack Lite) takes a different approach: the subscriber has only an IPv6 address and IPv6 connectivity. IPv4 traffic is tunneled to an Address Family Transition Router (AFTR) in the operator's network, which decapsulates and translates to reach IPv4 servers. This eliminates IPv4 address assignment at the CPE layer but requires IPv6 to be rock-solid, since IPv4 now depends on it. NAT64 provides IPv6-only subscribers with access to IPv4 content via stateful translation and DNS64, requiring minimal translation infrastructure.
sections.plainLanguage: As IPv4 addresses become scarce, operators can either share addresses among many customers (CGN) or stop giving IPv4 addresses at all, tunneling IPv4 traffic when needed (DS-Lite).

sections.title: Operational Considerations
sections.content:
IPv6 transition creates several operational challenges. Organizational experience is low: staff need training on IPv6 concepts, routing, troubleshooting, and monitoring. Service management systems must track both IPv4 and IPv6 addresses, prefixes, and dynamic assignments. Transition technologies can degrade performance: tunneling increases overhead, changes packet size, and adds latency. Suboptimal routing may occur if translation devices are not on the natural traffic path.

Operators should prefer native routing (no tunneling or translation) for dominant traffic. In early phases, IPv6 traffic is low, so tunneled access is acceptable. As IPv6 grows, native dual stack becomes essential. Operators must also manage CPE lifecycle and ensure customer-facing equipment supports planned technologies before wide deployment.
sections.plainLanguage: Teams need training, tools need updates, and old equipment might not support new features. Operators must plan these changes as carefully as they build the new infrastructure.

sections.title: The IPv6-Only Endgame
sections.content:
The final vision is an IPv6-only access network where subscriber CPEs receive only IPv6 addresses and prefixes. The operator's core network runs both IPv6 and IPv4, providing native IPv6 to all subscribers. IPv4 content access is mediated by DS-Lite (for applications and devices that demand IPv4 connections) or NAT64 (for reaching legacy IPv4 servers without per-device tunnels).

This model simplifies the access layer (single IP version) but requires IPv6-capable CPE hardware and applications. Viability increases as consumer equipment is replaced with IPv6-capable versions. NAT64 deployments will eventually reduce translator load as more content migrates to IPv6. This phase is not intended to happen quickly, but operators should design their networks now to avoid making IPv6 dependent on IPv4 infrastructure, which would constrain the network's eventual transition.
sections.plainLanguage: Eventually, when old devices are gone, the access network can be purely IPv6, and special gateways will translate when anyone needs to reach IPv4-only servers. This is simpler and more modern.
